newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire rebels conduct business as peace moves stall.
newsitem.headline: Zaire rebels conduct business as peace moves stall.

text.p: The rebel alliance in control of the richest half of Zaire said on Wednesday that companies were lining up to secure business with the men they expect will soon be the country's new leaders.

With plans for top-level talks on a peaceful transition of power apparently stalled, the rebels were carrying on with preparations for a military showdown -- but also taking care of business for the future.

Financial commissioner (finance minister) Mawana Nanga Mawanpanga said the rebels had been visited by South African mining houses Anglo American, De Beers and JCI, together with investment bank Investec.
Other companies beating a path to Lubumbashi included Arab Contractors and Banro Resource.

"There are plenty of companies coming. Yesterday we had a marathon day of talks," he told Reuters at his temporary headquarters in the Bank of Zaire building in the country's second largest city, capital of mineral-rich Shaba province.
"When the minerals are in the ground they don't serve anybody. We want production to create income and jobs for our people."
Many of these companies already had dealings in Zaire with the now tottering government of President Mobutu Sese Seko, the man the rebels vow to topple before June.
Mawanpanga said that De Beers, the company that controls the world diamond market, had conceded in talks that it would open up the trade to more buyers.
"This was very good progress in high-stakes negotiations," he said.

The rebel Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire, led by Laurent Kabila, last week awarded a $1 billion mineral exploitation contract to America Mineral Fields, to the disappointment of rival South African bidders, including Anglo American.
Mawanpanga said he had told Anglo executives that the rebels were satisfied they had awarded the contract to the highest bidder.
The most immediately lucrative part of the deal was the contract to process thousands of tonnes of copper-cobalt tailings at Kolwezi, Mawanpanga said.
"You don't have to dig it up, it's there waiting to be turned into metal."
There were six executive jets at Lubumbashi airport on Wednesday, and businessmen from various countries could be seen at the main hotel talking on cell phones or discussing prospectuses.
Kabila remained in seclusion at a villa on the city's edge. With no concrete sign of negotiations to end the civil war, his Alliance was continuing its preparations to take the capital, Kinshasa.
